extracted.intended_audience: Informed citizens, framers, and voters of New York (general public interested in constitutional design)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles and practical rules for structuring a republican (federal) government to preserve liberty by preventing encroachments among branches, securing minority rights, and ensuring representative dependence on the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid occasional appeals to the people for resolving inter-departmental encroachments
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on ad hoc or occasional appeals to the people (conventions called when two of three departments concur by two-thirds) as the primary safeguard against encroachments between departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons given: such appeals may fail when two departments combine against the third; frequent appeals imply defects and erode reverence for government; appeals inflame public passions and party spirit so the decisions would be driven by passion not reason; conventions would likely be populated by members or allies of the department under scrutiny, biasing outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of periodical (scheduled) appeals to the people as a corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodic appeals (e.g., reviews at fixed intervals) are also an inadequate means to enforce constitutional boundaries between departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If intervals are short, reviews are subject to the same partisan distortions as occasional appeals; if distant, abuses will have become entrenched and remedial review will be ineffectual; distant censure is a weak restraint on present excesses. The Pennsylvania 'Council of Censors' experiment is cited as illustrating partisanship and inefficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of government must provide internal checks and balances
rubrics_metrics.description: The government's internal structure must be contrived so that constituent parts keep each other in proper places, supplying what exterior provisions cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exterior remedies (appeals to people) are inadequate; instead, contrive the interior relations among departments so that mutual relations serve as checks. General observations include creating rival interests and structural devices so each office is a check on the others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each department should have a will of its own
rubrics_metrics.description: Each branch should be constituted so its members have an independent will and minimal ability to appoint members of the other branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideally all appointments would come independently from the people through channels with no communication; practical deviations may be necessary (see judiciary exceptions). The aim is to prevent one department from dominating appointments and thereby subverting independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow practical exceptions for judiciary appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: The strict rule of wholly separate appointment channels may be relaxed for the judiciary due to necessary qualifications and permanence of tenure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peculiar qualifications are essential for judges (justifying different selection modes), and permanent tenure soon destroys dependence on appointing authority; thus the judiciary warrants practical accommodation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Members of each department should be independent in emoluments
rubrics_metrics.description: Members should be as little dependent as possible on other branches for the emoluments (compensation) attached to their offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the executive or judiciary are dependent on the legislature for their pay or emoluments, then their independence is nominal. Financial independence is necessary to preserve independence in other respects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design incentives so ambition counters ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: Use opposing and rival interests—structural incentives—so that personal interest (ambition) motivates officials to defend constitutional rights of their office against encroachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The private interest of each individual should act as a sentinel over public rights. This matches the maxim 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition' and is a general device repeated throughout distributions of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide the legislature into different branches
rubrics_metrics.description: Because legislative authority tends to predominate in republics, divide it into separate branches with different modes of election and principles of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different modes of election and separation reduce connection among branches and help check legislative predominance. Further precautions (e.g., fortifying the executive) might be necessary depending on relative weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortify a weak executive by qualified connections, not absolute negatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely solely on an absolute executive veto; consider qualified connections between the executive and the weaker branch of the legislature to support the executive's constitutional rights without detaching it from its own department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An absolute negative (veto) might be insufficient or abused; a qualified connection can lead the weaker branch of the legislature to support the constitutionally weaker department when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federalism gives a double security to rights
rubrics_metrics.description: In a compound republic, dividing authority between federal and state governments and then subdividing allotted powers among departments provides a double security for the rights of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different governments will control each other while each is controlled internally; the federal device reduces the danger of oppressive majorities within narrow jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure minority rights by multiplying interests and classes
rubrics_metrics.description: To protect minorities from majoritarian oppression, create many separate descriptions of citizens (interests, classes, sects) so unjust combinations of a majority become improbable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two methods exist: introduce an independent will (hereditary/self-appointed) or multiply interests within society. The latter is preferred in a federal republic; multiplicity of interests and sects increases security and depends on extent of country and population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Larger (but practicable) republics are better able to self-govern
rubrics_metrics.description: A larger society, within a practical sphere, is more capable of self-government because it contains more diverse interests and sects that prevent oppressive majorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extending the sphere is feasible via a judicious modification of federal principles; larger territory encourages multiplicity of interests and stability of republican government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define suffrage (right of electors) in the Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The convention should define the qualifications of electors (right of suffrage) in the Constitution rather than leaving it to Congress or State legislatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaving suffrage to Congress would be improper because the definition is fundamental to republican government; leaving it to States would make the federal branch too dependent on state governments. Fixing the rule conforms to standards already established by states and is not easily alterable by states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for Representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: A Representative must be at least 25 years old, have been a citizen for seven years, be an inhabitant of the state when elected, and hold no office under the United States during service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These reasonable limitations open the door to merit regardless of native/adoptive status, age beyond minimum, wealth, or religious profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biennial elections for the House balance dependence and stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent elections (biennial) secure the House's dependence on and sympathy with the people while avoiding dangers of excessively frequent or infrequent elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience from British, Irish, colonial, and state examples suggests biennial elections are neither dangerous nor insufficient; the federal legislature has less supreme authority than the British Parliament, so shorter duration for more powerful bodies is recommended. Historical examples (Britain's evolution, Ireland, colonial America, Virginia) are used to justify biennial periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorial or review bodies are prone to partisanship and inefficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies created to review past administrations (e.g., Pennsylvania's Council of Censors) are likely to be partisan and ineffective in altering established legislative practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The council's members were active in prior administrations and parties; proceedings were split into fixed violent parties and decisions often misconstrued limits rather than constrained abuses. Contemporary legislatures sometimes ignore such councils' constructions, showing the remedy's inefficacy.
